Tax ancient worship of that Bon of Apollo, to whom gifts of healing and the patronage of medicine were divinely entrusted, find its latest embodiment and its truest antitype in the event which is chronicled in our columns of today. No statue of dEsculapius, with serpent-wreathed staff, -surmounts the en- trance or adorns the penetralia of the fine building in li eath.etreet ; it is true, never- theless, the same sad experiences of human pain and weakness, coupled with the desire to -mploy the resources which a beneficent Providence has stored in the womb o. nature audio the brain of man, find expression amid the whirr of modern machinery—so fraught with risk to health and limb—as those which dictated the consecration of a temple to the father of Hygeia in the year 462, after the fisinding of Rome. Grati- tude inspired the not in the latter cam, as in the former. "The plague" had disap- peared after visiting both sides of the Tiber, and small pox halt, no far, spared the banks of the Mersey. Yet, as an elements! selfish- ness mingles itself alike with our tams and our prayers, gratitude may here be said to consist very largely in "a lively 8011b0 of favours to come." We are slowly learning the lesson which plague and Providence conspire to teach, that disease and infirmity are the offspring of vim, profligacy, filth, and idleness. Helen may study and write; Hip- prorates may ply his knife and watery ; but only a life which fulfils the predeetined con- ditions of human rest and activity can secure an increased immunity from mental and physical anguish. Ass nation we have our peculiar offences against the laws of health sine against the body," as the Apostle Paul mills them—to answer for and amend. Our Eumenides are not far to seek, either. The snaky furies beneath whose avenging both vast herds of our miserable fellow- mortals are driven, may be identified in our streets and alleys any hour of any day. Mr. Crone struck a key-note which might be prolonged indefinitely —prolonged indeed to the confusion of those who think that the people only want "more Bishops' and "religious education" to transform them into a sober, thrifty, pious, and altogether admirable race. 0 IMICia simplsoitaa! What ' care Tom, Dick, and Harry, about points of I recondite dogma which never touch their vital interests? Even the zealous mob which applied, so to speak, the forceps more: vigorously than politely or kindly to a cer- tain very troublesome "Tooth" the other day,l oared much lees about the ostensible griev- anoe of ritualistic masquerade, than about " the defiance of popular sentiment and con- trol which the whole thing implies. They: know that the posture is a sacerdotal one ; that the income symbolises the flattery which is the breath of Anglican nostrils ; that copes end chasubles are the eheepie clothing : under which the wolf hidee. And while clever men laugh those who are also judi- cious cannot but grieve at the injury done to morals and religion alike by this exalta. tion of the mint, anise and ouramin over the weightier matters of the law. Alas : Ignorance is still the prolific parent I of our social evils, though we boast the grandest etvilisation which man has yet attained. Crime, her eldest daughter, Mill tempts the pauper-born to war against pro. party and privilege in which they have no share. Our colossal prisons testify to the fact that our restraints are largely unmoral, often, indeed, immoral. The moat hideous of the modern furies--clrunkennees—is the lu,tinat of them all. And as it is mainly the product of the common neglect, the common life suffers, and the common purse pays for it. Disease follows hard upon the footsteps of her twin-sister. The "-lower orders," as they are celled, with unconscious irony are, for the most part, epawned on mud-banjos which accumulate, like offal-heaps, around the abodes of luxury. Paupers and criminals breed pauperism and crime. Hence the need—which Mammon itself cannot safely ignore—for fever-wards within which conta- gious disease may be stilled; for Hoe. pitals which may snatch the helplessly- prostrated from the impending fate; for Dispensaries where medioal aid can be had by the poor and unfortunate, to whom Society still owes the natural debt. In rearing the noble structure which the Home Secretary opened— some of our wealthier townspeople have done themeelves lasting honour. Let it be the care of the community that the institution shall effect ',lasting good. The time has happily gone for ever by when it could be truthfully said that the profession throw "drugs of which they knew tittle, into a body of which they know lees." But the time has not gone by for a vigilant supervi- sion of "Charities" which are largely abused by improvident people, who waste their time, money, and stamina in sensual indulgence, and then—without one purpose of amend- ment —hold out the hand to receive the dote of the benevolent. We believe this point to be one of supreme importance, and shall re- turn to it at some future time. Suffice it to say now, in concluding this cursory glance at a great subject, that this latest recogni- tion of a public duty of the most sacred character, lays a still heavier responsitffity upon all those who assume the functions of local government and instruction. What if rulers and teachers come short in their knowledge of the oracles which reveal a people's destiny Laws of nature will not swerve from their course to gratify either pride or piety. Mitred clergy may ordain fasts, and cry for deliverance from " plague, pestilence, and famine," while retribution stays not her hand—calmly demanding, "Is this such %feat as I have chosen I to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke ?" The " Peculiar People" will go on praying instead of "resorting to the physi. mans" ; until the light of knowledge has driven away the earthborn superstitions of the past; and then—in a universe of divine law, which has quietly taken the place of the false conception of a chaos tilled by warning powers, the healing art will once more assume its rightful place ; the Good Physician will be honoured for what he is, not for what he is not; Saviour will again signify healer—as it did in Saxon daye ;"a sound mind in a sound body" will be the supreme desideratum; the vital, and not merely the etymological relationship of health and holiness will be fully expounded. In that day the old gospel "Wash you, lake you clemon !" will be honoured—not in I the breach but in the observance. Once more, "fine linen, clean and white," will appropriately symbolise "tae righteousness of the saints."

the following review of Mr. Cobden's famous pamphlet entitled " Russia, by a Manchester Manufacturer—a work made newly remarkable by the recent public quotation of it by Mr. Cobden's illuatri- ous colleague in the crusade of English Free Trade—is sent for publication in the Examiner, by a veteran Reformer, near Warrington, who took part in the early conflicts, and shared the later victories of Liberalism, when Liberalism represented a policy of combat, and its disciples re- ceived and wore proud of the palm of obloquy and social persecution. • II arm, in former notices, of what is called the Eastern QUOlotioll, referred at length to Mr. Cobilen's excellent pamphlet on the state of Turkey as it was forty years ago, since which time idawithetandiug the eup- port given her by France and lingland, she has sunk deeper and deeper in the gulf of crime and bankruptcy, we may now proceed, after her rejection of the proposals of the late Conference and her defiance of European opinion, to consider the future of that im- portant question. Thanks to the late ex- pression of an earnest and enlightened public opinion there is now little danger of our rulers repeating the madnese of another Crimean war to support the "sick man" in hie vicious course. That policy it may now be aseunied is for ever abandoned, and the Government of Turkey moot now and al no meet its inevitable destiny, and that des- tiny appears to us to be toe entire disinte- gration of her power and empire. Russia, in accordance with presumed traditional policy may, and probably will, enter into the struggle, but, unaided by the active co- operation of the provinces, Rueeia will be unable to subdue them. The conquest and annexation a Constantinople we hold to be impossible, and the annexation of any of the provinces is equally—from the many surrounding circumstances—moot improb- able. Yet many of our alarmists assume the conquest of Constantinople to be an easy matter, and predict the predominance of Russia in the Mediterranean to the perma- nent injury of Southern Europe, overlook- ing entirely the great anginal. of Toulon and Malta, and, as we pointed out before, the great influence of free, united, and powerful Italy, and the rising power and civilisation of modern Greece, all which are pow ertul obstacles to such aggrandiaemeat. Rotor' ring to the power of trussia, Mr. Cobden re- markethat "the autocrat °Jaime, the allegiance of people of every ratio, tongue, and religion, tribes or Cosmos and of Tartary, wandering over the low countries of the Cower's, Cir- eseaians, Mingrelians, with more than thirty other tribes, some Christians, others Ma- hametan, who are wholly or partially sub- dued by the Czar. If the best interests of Russia were understood (tie they are now be- ginning to be) she should cease the wars of the sword, and begin the battle with the wildernese by constructing railroad., build- ing bridges, foetering the accumulation of capital, the growth of cities, and the increase of freedom and civiliaation, the only sources of power and wealth." Yat, husaia insol- vent and impoverished, by the government of her unwieldy empire, anhnoet without ii fleet and the means of manning one, is be- lieved by our alarmists to meditate the inva- sion of India by the Suez Canal; an alarm utterly unreasonable, and a project which our space will not permit us to show is im- possible. Another cry is being continually I raised that our Eastern Empire is widen • I gored by Russian advances in Central Asia. We hold that the barren steppes, the track- less deserts of there regions, with the mighty Himalayas, must for ever bar her progress in that direction, even were it her policy and • wish to enter on that stupendous enterprise. All her extensions there over barbarous and • semi-barbarous tnbes have only been to her . a source of weakness, and her greatest ener- • gies must long be required to keep them in! subjection. Ear different is now tho case of • our Eastern Empire, composed as it is also ! .of many and different patrons and people; they all repose with advantage under the I paternal government of Great Britain, and whilst that government is continued in India I for India'a good, it may be safely asserted that it will endure until that dietant period : when it is to be hoped she will be able by the advancement and education of her people, to enter coins difficult task of her own self ' government. This is not the place to ask ! what no statesman or public writer—as far se we are aware ol—has demonstrated. What beuefit, if any, does England derive from the poeseesion of that vast Empire? Her interests, as Mr. Cobden has ably proved, and as we shall recapitulate, are other interests. Returning, therefore. to our preeent subject, it may now be conoidered as certain that the powers who entered into the late abortive conference are bound in • honour for the better government, a prospec- tive independence of the afflicted; provinces , of Turkey, and the deliverance of their Chris- , flan population from Mahomedan tyranny • and injustice, to take furrther energetic action for those purposes, and it will be the 1 duty of England to countenanee every judi- cious effort which they may make in fur- ! then/nee of three great objects. But we I utterly repudiate the doctrine that it is the • duty or the interest of England to enter into I war, even for those °bluetit. The only true interests of England amend now as as ever in the' diffusion of the blessings of I Christianity, the peaceful extension ot her commerce, the further development of her vast manufacturing industry, the propaga- tion of the principles of peace, and the sett- ing before the world an enduring example of those mighty agencies in the happiness I and contentment of a sober, honest, educated and intelligent people. We earnestly re- commend the careful consideration of Mr. Cobden's excellent pamphlet "Russia," though forty eventful years have posited over it, though hobo dead he yet speaketh. And we conclude this lengthy retrospect, in the repetition ahm ova words. "In the name oi every artisan 01 the kingdom, to whom war would bring the tidings once more of ' Guttering and despair, in the behalf of the I peasantry of theta Islands, to whom the first cannon would sound the knell of yrivation and death, on the part of the merchants, manufacturers, and traders, who can expect no other fruits from hostilities but bank- I ruptcy and ruin, in a word for the sake of ! the vital interersta of these and all other I classes of the community, we solemnly pro- I test against Great Britain being plunged I into war with Russia or any other country, In defence of Turkey, a war which, whilst it ' . would inflict disasters upon every portion of I 1 the community, could not bestow a perms- I nem benefit upon any class of it; and even I upon our slimes, in which no part of the civilized world would have cause to rejoice. I I Having the interests of all orders of Society to support our arguments in favour of peace' we need not dread war. These and not the piques of diplomatiste, the whims of crowned ! heads, the intrigues of ambassadreeses, or I schoolboy rhetoric on the balance of power, will henceforth determine the Foreign policy of our Government. That policy will be ! based on the bona-fide principle of non-in- terventiou in the political affairs of other nations, and from the moment this maxim becomes the lode star, by which our Govern- ment shall steer the vessel of the state, from that moment the good old ship Britannia will float triumphantly in smooth and deep water, and the rocks, shoals, and hUrfiaalloll of foreign war are Snared i9C OTINi"
